title: Contradictory Demands Are Everywhere in Teaching
author: Rod Naquin
summary: Rod Naquin uses organizational-paradox theory (Smith and Lewis, 2011) to reframe a familiar teaching-coaching puzzle: why a student teacher responds to an identical-seeming situation quickly on Monday and lets it sit until Friday, arguing this is not inconsistency but a genuine, unresolvable tension between learning-facing and adult-facing demands that has to be renegotiated constantly rather than balanced once. He distinguishes paradox from dilemma precisely, a dilemma is a one-time choice that sticks, while a paradox recurs because any resolution is only temporary, and situates the parent-email pattern within Smith and Lewis's four paradox families as simultaneously a belonging paradox (loyalty to one student versus the wider community of adults) and an organizing paradox (a teaching day structurally cannot run instruction and communication at full attention at once). Citing Poole and Van de Ven's and Sundaramurthy and Lewis's research, he argues these contradictions are built into how organizations function rather than dysfunctions a well-run system eventually eliminates, and that boards or teams that try to permanently resolve such tensions in one direction perform worse than those that deliberately cycle between poles. His practical payoff is a specific coaching move: instead of asking whether a decision was right, ask what the person was protecting when they made it and whether they noticed doing so, since a teacher who can articulate the trade-off is managing the tension deliberately (a virtuous cycle) while one who cannot is merely reacting under pressure.
points: Precisely distinguishes paradox from dilemma using Smith and Lewis's framework: a dilemma is a one-time choice that sticks, while a paradox recurs because any resolution is only ever temporary, reframing 'inconsistent' teacher behavior as a category error in how it's being judged.

Classifies the specific parent-email-versus-student-attention tension as simultaneously a belonging paradox (individual student loyalty versus wider adult-community accountability) and an organizing paradox (a teaching day structurally cannot run instruction and communication at full attention simultaneously), giving the vague feeling of being pulled in two directions a named, theorized structure.

Cites Poole and Van de Ven's (1989) and Sundaramurthy and Lewis's governance research to argue organizational contradictions are built-in features, not dysfunctions to be engineered away, and that boards attempting to permanently resolve such tensions in one direction consistently underperform those that keep both poles in play.

Distinguishes a 'vicious cycle' (defensively picking one side and treating the other as the enemy) from a 'virtuous cycle' (deliberately cycling between poles on purpose) as the difference between managing a paradox well and merely reacting to it under pressure.

Converts the theory into a specific, reusable coaching question - not 'was that the right call' but 'what were you protecting when you made it, and did you know you were weighing it' - designed to surface whether a teacher's inconsistent-looking behavior reflects deliberate trade-off management or unexamined reaction.
quotes: There's the learning-facing pull, the kid who's stuck, the group that needs support right now. And there's the adult-facing pull, the parent email, the colleague who needs five minutes, the team meeting where you're supposed to show up. Both are real, both are constant, and neither one goes away because the other one is loud.

Contradictory yet interrelated elements that exist simultaneously and persist over time, elements that seem logical when considered in isolation but irrational, inconsistent, and even absurd when juxtaposed.
A dilemma is a one-time choice, weigh it, pick, move on, the choice sticks. A paradox is different because any choice is only temporary.
Poole and Van de Ven made this point back in 1989: contradictions like this are built into how organizations function, not signs of dysfunction to be engineered away.

Sundaramurthy and Lewis later showed the same pattern in corporate governance, boards that tried to resolve the control-versus-collaboration tension once and for all, in one direction, consistently did worse than boards that kept both in play.

A vicious cycle, you pick a side defensively, dig in, and treat the other pole as the enemy. A virtuous cycle, you accept the tension as real and permanent, and you move back and forth between the poles on purpose instead of freezing into one.
Instead of asking someone to defend a decision, ask what they set aside to make it, and whether they noticed doing it.
